paragraphs.heading: The farthest spacecraft
paragraphs.text: Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe launched on September 5, 1977, 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2. It was sent to study the outer Solar System and then the interstellar space beyond the Sun's heliosphere. As of October 2026 it is 172.52 AU, or about 25.8 billion km, away. No other object made by people is farther from Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Jupiter, Saturn and Titan
paragraphs.text: On its way out it flew past Jupiter, Saturn and Titan, Saturn's largest moon. NASA had to choose between a flyby of Pluto or one of Titan. Titan won because it was known to have a substantial atmosphere. The probe looked at the weather, rings and magnetic fields of both gas giants, and it was the first probe to send back detailed pictures of their moons.

paragraphs.heading: Into interstellar space
paragraphs.text: Its extended mission, shared with Voyager 2, is to find and study the outer edges of the heliosphere and to start exploring the interstellar medium. On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause and became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Two years later the Sun's coronal mass ejections hit it in a third wave that lasted until at least December 15, 2014. That gave more evidence that it really was in interstellar space.

paragraphs.heading: How it is built
paragraphs.text: Voyager 1 was built by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Its main body is a ten-sided prism. It carries 11 science instruments, plus 16 hydrazine thrusters and gyroscopes that help keep its radio antenna pointed at Earth. That antenna is a 3.7-meter dish that sends and receives radio waves through the three Deep Space Network stations on Earth. Power comes from three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) filled with plutonium-238, which made about 470 W at launch.

paragraphs.heading: Running down slowly
paragraphs.text: By 2025 its signals took more than 23 hours to reach Earth, and it is projected to reach one light day from Earth on November 18, 2026. The power from its RTGs drops over time as the fuel decays and the thermocouples wear out. As of 2026 only two instruments still work: the Plasma Wave Subsystem and the magnetometer. The RTGs may give enough power to send engineering data until 2036.

paragraphs.heading: Reviving old thrusters
paragraphs.text: In 2017 the team fired the spacecraft's trajectory correction thrusters for the first time since 1980, which let the mission run two to three years longer. Several more thrusters were brought back into use in 2018, 2019 and 2025. The extended mission is expected to keep returning science for several more years.
